p1.key: Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> has ionic bonding between Na<sup>+</sup> and CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup> and covalent bonds within the carbonate ion. MgBr<sub>2</sub> is purely ionic; CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> and CH<sub>3</sub>COOH are purely covalent.

MgBr<sub>2</sub> contains only Mg<sup>2+</sup> and Br<sup>−</sup> ions. NaNO<sub>3</sub> and NH<sub>4</sub>Cl contain polyatomic ions with covalent bonds inside them, and H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is covalent.
Lattice enthalpy increases with ionic charge (stronger attraction) and decreases as the ions get bigger (greater separation). Only I causes an increase.
X (4s2, calcium) loses 2 electrons to form X2+; Y (3p5, chlorine) gains 1 electron to form Y−. Balancing charges gives XY2.
Forming a lattice from gaseous ions is strongly exothermic (A and C are endothermic). LiF has smaller ions than NaCl (both 1+/1−), so stronger attraction and the more negative value.
Sodium (group 1) loses its single outer electron to form Na<sup>+</sup>; each oxygen atom gains two electrons to form O<sup>2−</sup>, not one.
Aluminium (group 13) forms Al<sup>3+</sup>, so each Al atom loses three electrons; each S atom gains two to form S<sup>2−</sup>, giving Al<sub>2</sub>S<sub>3</sub>.
Lattice enthalpy (IB convention) is the enthalpy change for 1 mol of solid ionic compound separating into gaseous ions: MgS(s) → Mg<sup>2+</sup>(g) + S<sup>2−</sup>(g).
Lattice enthalpy increases with stronger electrostatic attraction between ions: higher ionic charges and smaller ionic radii (ions closer together).

NH<sub>4</sub>Cl contains NH<sub>4</sub>⁺ and Cl⁻ ions (ionic bonding) and covalent N–H bonds (including a dative bond) within the ammonium ion. MgCl<sub>2</sub> is ionic only; HCl and H<sub>2</sub>CO are covalent only.
Group 2 forms X²⁺ ions and group 6 (16) forms Y²⁻ ions. The charges balance 1 : 1, giving XY.
Attraction between ions increases with ionic charge and decreases with distance between ion centres, so high charge and small size give the greatest lattice enthalpy.
Solid ionic compounds (CaO(s)) do not conduct because the ions are fixed in the lattice. Molten NaF and aqueous KI have mobile ions; graphite has delocalized electrons.
These are reverse lattice enthalpies. Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ are doubly charged and smaller than Ca²⁺ and S²⁻, so forming MgO from its gaseous ions releases the most energy.
Mg²⁺ and N³⁻ balance as 3 × (+2) = 2 × (−3): Mg<sub>3</sub>N<sub>2</sub>. Al³⁺ and S²⁻ balance as 2 × (+3) = 3 × (−2): Al<sub>2</sub>S<sub>3</sub>.
Ionic bonds form when there is a large electronegativity difference, typically between a metal (which loses electrons to form cations) and a non-metal (which gains electrons to form anions).
Ca²⁺ and O²⁻ are doubly charged (charge product 4, vs 1 for LiF and LiI), and O²⁻ is smaller than S²⁻. So CaO has the highest lattice enthalpy.

Lattice enthalpy depends on the electrostatic attraction between ions, which increases with ionic charge and decreases with ionic radius. The ionization energy needed to form the ion does not affect the lattice enthalpy itself. A: I and II only.

All four compounds have 1+/1− charges, so the smallest ions give the strongest attraction. Na+ is smaller than K+ and F− is smaller than Cl−, so NaF has the largest (most endothermic) lattice enthalpy. C.

Lattice enthalpy increases with ionic charge and decreases with ionic radius. 1+/1− compounds are lowest, with KCl < NaCl (K+ larger). 2+/2− compounds are highest, with MgS < MgO (S2− larger). Order: KCl < NaCl < MgS < MgO.
Electrostatic attraction ∝ product of charges / distance between ion centres, so small ions with high charge give the largest lattice enthalpy. A.

Lattice enthalpy increases with ion charge and decreasing ion size. MgO has 2+/2− ions, and Mg<sup>2+</sup> is smaller than Ca<sup>2+</sup>, so it has the strongest attraction and the greatest lattice enthalpy.
Nitrate NO<sub>3</sub>⁻, phosphate PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3−</sup>, carbonate CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup>, ammonium NH<sub>4</sub>⁺: only row C has all four correct.

Mg<sub>3</sub>N<sub>2</sub> is formed from a reactive metal and a non-metal with a large electronegativity difference: Mg<sup>2+</sup> and N<sup>3−</sup> ions. Al<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>6</sub> and SF<sub>6</sub> are covalent molecules, and SiO<sub>2</sub> is a covalent network.

Nitrate is NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>, sulfate SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>, phosphate PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3−</sup> and hydrogencarbonate HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>. NO<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> is nitrite and SO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup> is sulfite.
Lattice enthalpy increases with ionic charge and decreases with ionic radius. Small ions with high charges give the strongest electrostatic attraction.

Mg<sup>2+</sup> has a higher charge and smaller radius than Na<sup>+</sup>, and Cl<sup>−</sup> is smaller than Br<sup>−</sup>. The strongest attraction, and so the most positive lattice enthalpy, is in MgCl<sub>2</sub>.

Calcium forms Ca<sup>2+</sup> and nitride is N<sup>3−</sup>. Balancing the charges needs 3 Ca<sup>2+</sup> (+6) for 2 N<sup>3−</sup> (−6): Ca<sub>3</sub>N<sub>2</sub>. C is calcium nitrite and D is calcium nitrate.

NaF (Na<sup>+</sup>, F<sup>−</sup>) and NH<sub>4</sub>NO<sub>3</sub> (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>, NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>) are ionic lattices, even though the polyatomic ions contain covalent bonds. SiO<sub>2</sub> is a giant covalent network.
Lattice enthalpy is largest when the ions have high charges and small radii. Mg<sup>2+</sup> and O<sup>2−</sup> are both doubly charged and small, so MgO has the most endothermic lattice enthalpy.
GaPO4 contains PO43−, so gallium forms Ga3+. With SO42−, balancing charges (2 × +3 = 3 × −2) gives Ga2(SO4)3.

Lattice enthalpy increases with ionic charge and decreases with ionic size. CsCl (large +1 cation) is lowest, then NaCl, then MgCl2 (small 2+ cation); MgO (2+ and 2− ions, both small) is highest: CsCl < NaCl < MgCl2 < MgO.
NaCl has a 6:6 lattice: each Na+ ion is surrounded octahedrally by six Cl− ions, and each Cl− by six Na+.

Ionic bonding needs a large electronegativity difference, typically a metal with a non-metal. CsCl combines a very electropositive metal (Cs) with Cl. ClO<sub>2</sub>, SCl<sub>2</sub> and SiCl<sub>4</sub> contain only non-metals (or a metalloid) and are covalent.
Lattice enthalpy reflects the electrostatic attraction between ions. It is greatest for large ionic charges and a small sum of ionic radii, because the ion centres are then closest together.

NaNO<sub>3</sub> contains ionic bonding between Na<sup>+</sup> and NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>, and covalent N–O bonds within the nitrate ion. SiH<sub>4</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>CO are only covalent; Na<sub>2</sub>S is only ionic.
Lattice enthalpy is largest for highly charged, small ions. MgS and MgO both have 2+/2− ions, but O2− is smaller than S2−, so MgO has the largest lattice enthalpy.

I is false: lattice enthalpy decreases as ionic radii increase, because the ions are further apart. II is true: larger cations give weaker lattices and lower melting points. III is true: solubility depends on the balance between lattice and hydration enthalpies. Answer: II and III only.
Na2O is ionic: ions are fixed in the solid but mobile when molten, so it conducts only as a liquid. It is a basic oxide forming NaOH in water, so the solution has a high pH.
Magnesium forms Mg2+ and nitrogen forms N3−. Balancing charges: 3 × (+2) = +6 and 2 × (−3) = −6, so the formula is Mg3N2.
Carbonate is CO32−, so Ni must be +2 in NiCO3. Nickel has variable oxidation states, so the Roman numeral is needed: nickel(II) carbonate.
Li (1s22s1) loses its single outer electron to form Li+, which has the stable 1s2 configuration of helium. The number of protons never changes when ions form.

NaF is formed from a metal and the most electronegative non-metal (large electronegativity difference), so it is predominantly ionic. HCl is covalent; NH<sub>4</sub>Br and NaOH also contain covalent bonds within their polyatomic ions.
